analysis.one_liner: Creates military tribunals to try foreign terror suspects and blocks them from challenging their detention in federal courts.
analysis.headline: Passed the House 250–175 and the Senate 65–34, and became law on October 17, 2006.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill writes into law a system of military tribunals to try non-U.S. citizens accused of terrorism or war crimes, with a military judge, defense counsel, and limited appeals. It also does several things that shrink the role of ordinary courts: detainees lose the right to file habeas corpus petitions (the traditional way to challenge detention before a judge), no one can invoke the Geneva Conventions as a source of rights in any U.S. court, and the rules are applied retroactively to detention and interrogation practices going back to September 11, 2001. It also expands legal protection for U.S. government personnel involved in interrogations.
analysis.who_benefits: The executive branch gains a durable legal framework for detaining and trying foreign terrorism suspects without the ordinary criminal courts, plus retroactive protection for its interrogation practices and personnel. The Defense Department controls the procedures, and government personnel get required legal defense in cases arising from authorized interrogations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The executive branch and U.S. interrogators

how_it_helps.text: Creates a standing military commission system, authorized by the President and run by the Defense Department, with a military judge, detailed defense counsel, and required vote thresholds for conviction and sentences [S3][S5].
Bars statements obtained through torture from being used against an accused, and prohibits compulsory self-incrimination [S3][S5].
Requires the government to provide counsel to U.S. government personnel engaged in authorized interrogations [S3].
Lists specific, codified war crimes — including attacking civilians, taking hostages, torture, and rape — so the rules are written in statute rather than left to the executive alone [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Foreign detainees: they can no longer go to federal court to challenge their detention or their treatment, cannot invoke the Geneva Conventions in any U.S. court, may face hearsay evidence and proceedings closed to the public or evidence withheld from them on national-security grounds, and the rules apply retroactively to everything done since September 11, 2001.
analysis.who_pays_short: Non-citizen detainees held by the U.S.

drawbacks.text: The bill strips non-citizens of habeas corpus — the centuries-old right to have a court examine whether their detention is lawful — routing any review through a narrow, executive-created appeals process [S5].

No person in any U.S. court can invoke the Geneva Conventions as a source of rights, and it declares that meeting the narrower Detainee Treatment Act standards fully satisfies U.S. treaty obligations [S3].
Hearsay evidence is admissible, and the judge may admit classified evidence the accused never sees, exclude the accused from parts of his own trial, and close proceedings to the public [S5].
The rules apply retroactively to detention, treatment, and trials dating back to September 11, 2001, including to claims already pending in court [S3].

The government is shielded in practice: interrogators gain required legal representation and the bill defines cruel treatment in ways supporters said would protect U.S. personnel from liability for conduct short of torture [S3].

A fair-minded supporter would acknowledge the trade-off: the Supreme Court's Hamdan ruling had invalidated the prior commission system, and Congress needed to authorize some lawful trial framework — but this bill answered that need by removing court oversight for the people with the least power to contest it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill did create a real trial system with a judge, defense counsel, and appellate review, and it does bar torture-tainted testimony — genuine procedural protections that the prior ad hoc system lacked. But the core of the bill moves power away from independent courts and toward the executive: detention becomes much harder to challenge, treaty-based rights become unenforceable in court, and the protections are extended retroactively. The people affected are foreign detainees with no vote and little voice in American politics, while the benefits accrue to the government officials running the system.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 250–175 on September 27, 2006, the Senate passed it 65–34 on September 28, and President Bush signed it into law on October 17, 2006.

narrative.text: Introduced September 12, 2006, and rushed through committee: the Armed Services Committee ordered it reported 52–8 on September 13, and the Judiciary Committee — which split 20–19 — reported it on September 25, just thirteen days after introduction [S7].
It was placed on the Union Calendar on September 25, 2006, in time for a vote before the 2006 election recess [S7].
The House passed it 250–175 and the Senate passed it 65–34, and President Bush signed it on October 17, 2006 [S1][S7].

The bill's key provisions — the habeas strip, the Geneva Conventions bar, retroactivity, and the admissibility of hearsay and closed proceedings — were all retained in the version that became law [S3][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The executive branch is better off: it gained a legal framework for detention and trial under its own control, retroactive cover for past interrogation practices, and a court system where non-citizens cannot contest their treatment. The people who lost are the detainees themselves and, more broadly, anyone who values court oversight of executive detention power.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The executive branch and U.S. interrogators

for.name: Duncan Hunter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through the Armed Services Committee, which ordered it reported 52–8 on September 13, 2006 [S1][S7].

for.name: F. James Sensenbrenner
for.what_they_did: Original sponsor; his committee marked up and reported the bill (20–19) on September 25, 2006 [S5][S7].

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Pressed Congress to enact a military commissions law after the Supreme Court's Hamdan ruling invalidated the prior system, and signed the bill into law on October 17, 2006.

for.name: The Senate
for.what_they_did: Passed the companion military commissions bill on September 28, 2006, with bipartisan support.

against.name: Most House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Formed the bulk of the 175 no votes on final House passage of the Military Commissions Act.

against.name: Russ Feingold
against.what_they_did: Led Senate opposition to the provision stripping habeas corpus rights from non-citizen detainees and voted against final passage.

against.name: American Civil Liberties Union
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the bill, arguing the habeas strip and treatment standards violated constitutional and treaty-based rights.

sides.party_line_note: Republicans overwhelmingly backed the bill — it passed the House 250–175 and the Senate 65–34 — while most Democrats opposed it, though a substantial minority of Democrats in each chamber joined the majority in favor.

industries.industry: U.S. military and intelligence interrogation personnel
industries.note: The bill requires the government to provide counsel to personnel engaged in authorized interrogations and defines treatment standards in a way supporters said would shield them from liability for conduct short of torture. The cost of that protection falls on detainees who can no longer sue or seek habeas review.

The bill locks in executive control over who is an 'unlawful enemy combatant,' who gets tried and where, with review confined to a court system the executive largely shapes — and with federal courts barred from hearing detention challenges. It states explicitly that nothing limits the President's power to create battlefield commissions.

The bill strips courts of jurisdiction over detention claims and habeas petitions from military commission cases, and bars them from hearing Geneva Conventions arguments, removing judicial oversight that courts had exercised for two centuries.
